## Introduction

Baroreceptors are sensory nerve endings that function as mechanoreceptors and are stimulated by distension and stretching of the structures in which they reside. There are two types of baroreceptors: high-pressure arterial baroreceptors located in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch, and low-pressure cardiopulmonary receptors found in the atria, ventricles, and pulmonary vessels. High-pressure arterial baroreceptors provide rapid, short-term regulation of arterial blood pressure. Changes in their firing are transmitted to the medulla, which adjusts sympathetic and parasympathetic activity to alter heart rate, cardiac contractility, and vascular resistance. Low-pressure cardiopulmonary receptors monitor central blood volume and contribute to the regulation of fluid balance. Together, these receptors help maintain blood pressure within a stable physiological range.

## Cellular Level

At the cellular level, baroreceptor afferent neurons are primary sensory neurons whose cell bodies reside in the petrosal ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve and the nodose ganglion of the vagus nerve. Their sensory terminals are located primarily within the adventitia of the carotid sinus and aortic arch, where they detect changes in arterial stretch. Baroreceptor terminals contain stretch-activated ion channels, including PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, which have been shown to contribute to baroreceptor mechanotransduction. Mechanical deformation of the arterial wall opens these nonselective cation channels, allowing Na+ and Ca2+ to enter the sensory terminals. The resulting inward current depolarizes the membrane and generates a receptor potential. When the membrane reaches threshold, action potentials are initiated and transmitted through baroreceptor afferent fibers to the medulla oblongata.[1][2][3][4]

Baroreceptor afferent fibers can be broadly categorized into two main types based on their size and conduction properties: large myelinated A fibers and small unmyelinated C fibers. Myelinated A fibers conduct impulses rapidly through saltatory conduction and are particularly responsive to rapid, pulsatile changes in arterial wall stretch, allowing swift cardiovascular reflexes. Smaller unmyelinated C fibers conduct impulses more slowly and generally provide more sustained, tonic information about arterial pressure. Both fiber types contribute to baroreflex signaling and convey a heartbeat-synchronized, blood pressure–dependent pattern of activity to the medulla oblongata.[1][4]

Within the medulla oblongata, baroreceptor afferents terminate primarily in the NTS, where they release glutamate onto second-order neurons. The NTS sends excitatory projections to the caudal ventrolateral medulla, whose inhibitory neurons project to the rostral ventrolateral medulla—a major source of excitatory drive to sympathetic preganglionic neurons. Through this pathway, the NTS indirectly inhibits sympathetic output to the heart and blood vessels. The NTS also sends excitatory projections to cardiac parasympathetic neurons in the nucleus ambiguus. These neurons provide parasympathetic output to the heart through the vagus nerve.[5][4]

Through the coordinated regulation of sympathetic and parasympathetic activity, the medullary baroreflex pathway adjusts heart rate, cardiac contractility, and vascular resistance to buffer fluctuations in arterial pressure and maintain cardiovascular stability.[6][4][6]

## Organ Systems Involved

Baroreceptor-mediated regulation of blood pressure and blood volume depends on the coordinated activity of multiple organ systems, including the nervous, cardiovascular, renal, and endocrine systems.

Central Nervous System

Peripheral baroreceptor afferents convey sensory information from arterial and cardiopulmonary receptors to the medulla through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. The NTS integrates afferent input from arterial and cardiopulmonary receptors and projects to autonomic centers, including the caudal ventrolateral medulla, dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, and nucleus ambiguus. These projections coordinate sympathetic and parasympathetic output. Supramedullary centers, including the hypothalamus, insular cortex, and other cortical regions, provide modulatory control of long-term cardiovascular regulation and behavioral adaptation.[5][4]

Cardiovascular System

High-pressure arterial baroreceptors respond to changes in arterial pressure, producing reflex adjustments in heart rate and systemic vascular resistance. Low-pressure cardiopulmonary baroreceptors respond primarily to changes in central blood volume and cardiac filling and initiate reflex mechanisms that regulate blood volume.[9][4]

Renal System

Arterial and cardiopulmonary reflexes influence renal sympathetic nerve activity. Through this activity, the reflexes regulate renal blood flow, glomerular filtration, and renin release. Activation of atrial stretch receptors decreases renal sympathetic tone, promoting natriuresis and diuresis to reduce blood volume and maintain fluid balance.[4]

Endocrine System

Baroreceptor and cardiopulmonary reflexes modulate hormonal pathways affecting blood pressure and blood volume, including the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and vasopressin secretion. Atrial stretch is also associated with the release of atrial natriuretic peptide from atrial cardiomyocytes.[4][10]

Respiratory System

Baroreceptor afferents influence brainstem respiratory centers. Through their projections to the NTS, arterial and cardiopulmonary baroreceptors can modulate respiratory activity.[5][11]

## Function

Baroreceptors regulate mean arterial pressure via a negative feedback loop.

Baroreceptors regulate mean arterial pressure via a negative feedback loop. Arterial baroreceptors are tonically active, and increases in arterial blood pressure increase vessel-wall stretch and raise their firing rate. Increased afferent input to the NTS enhances parasympathetic outflow and inhibits sympathetic outflow to the heart and peripheral vasculature, leading to decreased heart rate and contractility, vasodilation, and decreased peripheral resistance. Conversely, decreases in blood pressure reduce baroreceptor firing, thereby reducing parasympathetic outflow and diminishing NTS-mediated inhibition of sympathetic outflow, resulting in increased heart rate and contractility, vasoconstriction, and increased arterial pressure.[1][9][4]

Cardiopulmonary baroreceptors, located in the atria, ventricles, and pulmonary vasculature, respond primarily to blood volume and filling pressures. An increase in blood volume increases receptor activity, promoting inhibition of renal sympathetic outflow and hormonal responses that enhance natriuresis and diuresis, thereby decreasing fluid volume. Conversely, a decrease in blood volume reduces receptor firing, leading to increased sympathetic tone in the heart, kidneys, and peripheral vasculature, together with activation of hormonal pathways, thereby promoting fluid conservation, maintaining cardiac output, and supporting blood pressure.[9][4][10]

Collectively, arterial and cardiopulmonary baroreceptors provide dynamic, integrated control of heart rate, vascular tone, blood volume, and organ perfusion, contributing to short-term blood pressure stability and longer-term regulation of blood volume and arterial pressure.[4][10][12]

## Mechanism

Baroreceptor mechanotransduction begins when distension of the carotid sinus or aortic arch deforms sensory nerve endings embedded within the vessel wall. This deformation opens mechanically activated, nonselective cation channels, including PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, producing a graded receptor potential. When the receptor potential reaches threshold, action potentials are generated, and their firing frequency varies with the magnitude and rate of stretch. Cardiopulmonary receptor endings are similarly activated by deformation of the atrial, ventricular, and pulmonary vascular walls.[2][3]

Carotid sinus afferents travel along the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and have their cell bodies in the petrosal ganglion. Aortic and cardiopulmonary afferents travel primarily through the vagus nerve, with their cell bodies located in the nodose ganglion. These afferents terminate in the NTS, where they release glutamate onto second-order neurons. NTS neurons activate the caudal ventrolateral medulla, whose GABAergic neurons inhibit sympathetic premotor neurons in the rostral ventrolateral medulla. Parallel NTS projections activate cardiac vagal neurons in the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus. Through these pathways, changes in mechanical stretch are converted into coordinated autonomic signals.[4][5][9]

Arterial baroreceptor firing depends on both the magnitude and rate of vessel wall stretch and adapts during sustained changes in arterial pressure. With persistent changes in pressure, the arterial baroreceptor pressure-response relationship shifts toward the prevailing pressure, a process known as resetting. This preserves sensitivity to transient fluctuations around the new operating pressure but reduces the baroreflex's ability to correct sustained pressure changes.[9][12][9]

## Pathophysiology

Baroreceptor dysfunction can result from adaptation to sustained hypertension, loss of afferent signaling, or an exaggerated response to carotid sinus stimulation.

Baroreflex Resetting and Reduced Sensitivity in Chronic Hypertension

In chronic hypertension, the arterial baroreflex resets to operate around the higher blood pressure. It continues to respond to short-term changes in pressure but becomes less effective at opposing the sustained elevation. Chronic hypertension can also cause arterial remodeling and stiffening, reducing deformation of the carotid sinus and aortic arch at a given change in pressure. This reduces changes in baroreceptor firing and further decreases baroreflex sensitivity.[12]

Afferent Baroreflex Failure

Damage to the afferent limb of the arterial baroreflex, particularly following head and neck radiation or surgery, can produce afferent baroreflex failure. Loss of reflex buffering results in marked blood pressure lability, including hypertensive surges, orthostatic hypotension, and syncope. Tachycardia may accompany hypertensive episodes.

Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity and Carotid Sinus Syndrome

At the opposite extreme, carotid sinus hypersensitivity is an exaggerated cardiovascular response to mechanical stimulation of the carotid sinus. When this response reproduces spontaneous symptoms such as presyncope or syncope, it is termed carotid sinus syndrome. Stimuli such as a tight collar, external neck pressure, or sustained head rotation may trigger the response. Carotid sinus activation increases cardiac vagal activity and withdraws sympathetic tone from the heart and vasculature. The abnormal response is classified into three hemodynamic subtypes according to which efferent component predominates:

Cardioinhibitory subtype: The cardiac vagal response predominates, producing marked bradycardia, atrioventricular block, or asystole. Blood pressure falls primarily because of the resulting decrease in cardiac output.

Vasodepressor subtype: Withdrawal of sympathetic vasomotor tone predominates, producing arterial vasodilation and venous pooling. Blood pressure falls because of decreased systemic vascular resistance and venous return, without marked slowing of the heart rate.

Mixed subtype: Both cardiac inhibition and sympathetic vasomotor withdrawal contribute substantially to the decrease in blood pressure.

Each subtype can reduce cerebral perfusion sufficiently to cause presyncope or syncope.[12][13]

## Clinical Significance

Baroreflex Resetting and Reduced Sensitivity

Baroreflex sensitivity can be measured during specialized cardiovascular or autonomic testing to quantify autonomic control. Reduced baroreflex sensitivity has prognostic value following myocardial infarction and in heart failure, although it is not routinely used as a stand-alone clinical test. Treatment focuses on managing the underlying hypertension, heart failure, or other cardiovascular disease.

Baroreflex activation therapy electrically stimulates the carotid sinus to modify autonomic activity. In the United States, it is approved to improve functional status, exercise capacity, and quality of life in selected patients with symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction despite guideline-directed therapy. Its use for resistant hypertension remains under investigation.[4][14]

Afferent Baroreflex Failure

Evaluation of suspected afferent baroreflex failure may include ambulatory or beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring and autonomic reflex testing. A history of head and neck radiation or surgery can help establish the diagnosis. Treatment aims to reduce the frequency and severity of blood pressure extremes rather than normalize blood pressure completely. Central sympatholytic medications may reduce hypertensive surges, while hydration, physical countermeasures, and selected blood pressure–raising medications may be used for hypotensive episodes.[15]

Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity and Carotid Sinus Syndrome

Carotid sinus massage can support the diagnosis of carotid sinus syndrome when it reproduces the patient’s spontaneous symptoms during continuous electrocardiographic and blood pressure monitoring. It should be performed only by trained clinicians and avoided in patients with a recent transient ischemic attack, stroke, or myocardial infarction or with known high-grade carotid stenosis.

Treatment begins with avoiding known triggers and reviewing medications that may worsen bradycardia or hypotension. Permanent cardiac pacing may be considered in selected patients with severe, recurrent cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome with documented asystole. Pacing is less effective in the mixed subtype and is not indicated for an isolated vasodepressor response because it does not restore vascular sympathetic tone.

Separately, carotid sinus massage may be used as a vagal maneuver to terminate atrioventricular node–dependent reentrant supraventricular tachycardia in hemodynamically stable patients. Other vagal maneuvers, particularly the modified Valsalva maneuver, are generally preferred.[16][17]
